Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

text:
Scrap the Parking Mandate

Every city that requires developers to build a fixed number of parking spaces with each new building is running an experiment on itself. The results are in, and they are not good. Minimum parking requirements should be removed from planning rules, and the sooner the better.

Start with what these rules actually are. They are not forecasts of demand. They are formulas, often borrowed from other cities or from a handbook of trip generation rates built on suburban sites with free parking. A restaurant must provide so many spaces per thousand square feet. An apartment block must provide two per unit, whether or not its future tenants own cars. Planners did not set these numbers by asking what the market would supply. They set them by assuming that every site should be able to absorb the peak demand for free parking on the busiest day of the year. No other part of the economy is planned on that logic.

The first cost is housing. A surface space takes roughly three hundred square feet once you count the aisles and ramps. A space in a structure can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space far more. Those costs do not vanish. They land in rents and sale prices, and they land on everyone, including households that own no car. Roughly a fifth of renting households in many American cities have no vehicle at all, yet they pay for parking inside their monthly rent. A mandate that forces a builder to include a space that a tenant does not want is a hidden tax on the poorest people in the building.

The second cost is the buildings that never get built. Parking minimums make small lots impossible to develop. A narrow infill site that could hold six apartments might hold only three once the required spaces are drawn on the plan. A corner shop that could reuse an old building cannot open, because the old building has no room for the required spaces. Historic main streets are full of such blocks, where the buildings are too beautiful to demolish and too constrained by code to reuse. The rule does not just add cost. It forbids whole categories of modest, incremental development.

The third cost is the shape of the city itself. When every building must be surrounded by asphalt, buildings spread apart, and distances grow. Walking becomes unpleasant and then impractical, so more people drive, so more parking is demanded, and the loop tightens. Studies of downtown land use have found astonishing shares of central land given over to storing cars, in some cases more area than goes to the buildings people actually live and work in. That land pays no property tax worth the name. A parking lot is a poor use of the most valuable ground a city has.

The strongest objection is practical. If cities stop requiring parking, will streets fill with cars and neighbours lose their patience? The evidence from places that have tried it says no. Buffalo scrapped its requirements citywide in 2017. Minneapolis, Seattle, San Francisco and a growing list of others have followed in whole or in part. Developers did not stop building parking. They built what they believed they could sell or rent, which in many neighbourhoods was still plenty, and in others was less. Projects came forward that had been stalled for years. The sky did not fall.

Removing the mandate is not the same as banning parking. This point is lost in almost every heated council meeting. A developer who knows that tenants in a suburban office park will drive will provide spaces, because a building with no parking there would sit empty. A lender will demand it. A tenant will demand it. What changes is that the decision moves from a formula in a municipal code to the people who bear the cost of getting it wrong. That is a much better place for it.

The remaining worry is spillover onto public streets. This is a real concern, but it is a problem with a pricing answer, not a mandate answer. Cities that manage on-street parking with permits, time limits or modest meter fees can keep curb space available without forcing every private owner to subsidise free storage. Some of the revenue can go back into the neighbourhood that generates it. A city that gives away its curb and then requires private builders to compensate for the shortage has the incentives backwards.

There is also a plain argument from fairness and freedom. Property owners ought to be allowed to build what they judge best for their land unless there is a clear public reason to stop them. Where is the public reason for a number of parking spaces? Noise, fire safety and structural soundness are public matters. How many cars a future tenant may bring is a private matter, to be settled among the tenant, the landlord and the lender.

A sensible reform is simple. Repeal the minimums entirely, rather than trimming them by a quarter or exempting a few districts. Keep sensible accessibility rules for disabled parking, since those serve a clear public interest. Let owners decide the rest. Price the curb. Watch what is built.

Cities spend enormous effort asking how to make housing cheaper, streets safer and downtowns livelier. Here is a reform that serves all three and costs the treasury nothing. The parking mandate was a well-meant guess made decades ago. It has been tested, and it has failed. Retire it.
